> 
> If we make requesting the sensor part of common code, at some point we could abstract that so an individual sensor implementation does not have to call this at all.

Requesting the name isn't unique to a sensor though. If we're going for abstraction and reuse, it should go in the common dbus class (where it already is). > 
> I have not seen any sensor reactor in this repo which does not request a bus name so i do not see the point of duplicating this call to each sensor reactor.

The reason to "duplicate" is requesting the name is actually an indication that init is complete, and all of dbus is populated.  Different applications find that at different times in their lifecycle, so it's kept separate.

> Requesting the name isn't unique to a sensor though. If we're going for abstraction and reuse, it should go in the common dbus class (where it already is). 

Abstractions without concrete examples often fall on deaf ears.
If we manage to establish a useful base class for what a `Reactor` is, maybe that can go some other repo long-term for re-use.

The point of this patch is broader than just requesting a name. It is for enabling the abstraction for Reactor code.

In reactors, there is an initialization phase, there is requesting a bus name.
We have various DBus matches, and configuration to deal with.

That's something each sensor has to deal with, and unlikely to change a lot in the near term.

> It's quite possible I'm not seeing the advantage here from code. Is there another refactor you're considering that would make this more clear?

If you want to do integration testing on a common code, you can make an example sensor which implements the interfaces expected by the common code.

Now the test coverage on the example sensor is *useless* since it is just a stub.

But it enables test coverage of the common code.

If we now maximize the amount of common code without hardware dependency ....
and minimize the amount of hardware specific code ...

then we can maximize the effective test coverage of our unit tests.

> The reason to "duplicate" is requesting the name is actually an indication that init is complete, and all of dbus is populated. Different applications find that at different times in their lifecycle, so it's kept separate.

That's a tradeoff between framework/library approach to common code.

If you approach common code as a framework, the common code calls into the sensor specific code.

If you approach common code as a library, the sensor specific code calls into the library.

When taking external dependencies, i usually prefer the library approach, since often no single dependency can assume role of being the framework in a complicated application.

But IMO if we can write both the framework (common code) and it's users (same repository), the 'framework' approach (common code calling into sensor specific code) is better,

since we often only have to get things right in a single source location.
We shouldn't reinvent asio::post in a different namespace.

The point here is to avoid having to pass `io` into it.

IMO this simplifies the API from the sensor perspective and makes the code more readable.

In this example of `hasManufacturingModeMatch' we are configuring a common code, and there are **only 2 possibilities.**

So there is only 1 mistake a sensor writer can make in this example.

(i am taking an abstract view here since i do not know the code details here as well as you do)

In contrast, if the sensor writer has to call this by themselves, they may fail to call it, call it in the wrong place, call it multiple times, ....

So with that approach there are more errors which can be made and also more different kinds of errors.

io_context is always global to an application.  It should not be owned by a single reactor class.

Conceptually you are right about this but the goal of `class Reactor` is to have a common code, avoiding code duplication.

It's possible to inherit from `Reactor` and then the application class will own it.

For example one could make `class ADCSensorManager` to inherit from `Reactor`
and then the application specific class could have a bunch of extra members vars for anything that's specific to that application.

By having a common code we can avoid subtle bugs arising due to different order of initialization and code drift.

From my perspective this practical concern outweighs a conceptual concern, but to each their own.

> Conceptually you are right about this but the goal of `class Reactor` is to have a common code, avoiding code duplication.
> 
> It's possible to inherit from `Reactor` and then the application class will own it.
> 
> For example one could make `class ADCSensorManager` to inherit from `Reactor`
> and then the application specific class could have a bunch of extra members vars for anything that's specific to that application.

That design of inheritance sounds very complex compared to just declaring an io_context (which is itself a large reusable interface) in main.  Having a class per application seems worse.

> 
> By having a common code we can avoid subtle bugs arising due to different order of initialization and code drift.

Lets be concrete when we talk about bugs.  Can you point to a bug or two of that nature that we've had on master and needed to fix?

> 
> From my perspective this practical concern outweighs a conceptual concern, but to each their own.

io_context being outside of main isn't conceptual.  It has caused crashes on shutdown in the past (check the dbus-sensors code history for some of the fixes).

>> By having a common code we can avoid subtle bugs arising due to different order of initialization and code drift.

> Lets be concrete when we talk about bugs. Can you point to a bug or two of that nature that we've had on master and needed to fix?

I can't say much about such bugs in dbus-sensors, this one is more based on my own experience.

Below is the most recent example of a bug based on code drift / lack of common code i have seen:

https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt/+/84841/comment/c35e497b_da3d20ce/

That one mostly incidental, and technically not even code drift (because they were probably created independently). Basically two fw update daemons are reading images which are encoded in a plain text format.

Due to lack of a common abstraction (line-based text file reader respecting both CR-LF and plain LF) there is now a fix which fixes an issue with carriage-return-line-feed sequence found on files created on M$ windows devices.

As opposed to plain `\n` found in files created on linux.

Having a common code would avoid the code drift (since the fix is currently only available to one of these updaters).

The image parser in question probably does not need to know what specific line ending sequence is used, and that can be broken out.

> io_context being outside of main isn't conceptual. It has caused crashes on shutdown in the past (check the dbus-sensors code history for some of the fixes).

ok, i guess your past experience has more weight in this matter, i brought back the io context to be stored separately in `main` function as before.
